# The evidence: what Jev actually scores

This is the most important file in this repo. The marketing says "40–200× faster,
mathematically cannot hallucinate." Both of those are true and **neither is about
accuracy.** Here is what independent measurement found.

## Read this first: the vendor's benchmark grades itself against other LLMs

TypeSafe's headline "Jev 67.8% vs GPT-Terra 67.9%" near-parity claim is measured as
**agreement with reference answers generated by averaging two other frontier models**
(reportedly GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1) — *not* against human-labeled ground truth.

That is a structurally biased metric. It measures "does Jev answer the way two big LLMs
answer", which is not the same as "is Jev right". Independent commentators flagged this as
the top methodological concern on launch day. **Do not inherit this methodology for your
own evals.**

Also worth noting: no number found anywhere — *including TypeSafe's own* — shows Jev being
**more accurate** than the models it is priced against. The best case in vendor material is
rough parity.

## Independent benchmark 1 — phishing email classification (Jev loses badly)

Source: `github.com/anisselbd/jev-phishing-bench`, n = 2,000 emails.

| Metric | Jev | Claude Haiku 4.5 |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | **62.6%** [60.5–64.7] | **81.3%** [79.5–82.9] |
| Recall (phishing caught) | **43.2%** | **76.4%** |
| AUROC | 0.689 | 0.837 |
| Expected Calibration Error | 0.154 | 0.097 |
| Label flips on identical repeat inputs | 2.2% | 0.7% |

Significant at McNemar p < 0.0001. Jev was **worse on accuracy, worse on recall, and worse
calibrated** than a small frontier LLM on a messy, realistic task.

And the detail that should make you pause before adopting anything: **a hand-written regex
heuristic scored 91.8%**, beating Jev's best individual signal question (89.4%, p=0.003).
For a well-understood, rule-expressible problem, plain code beat the AI outright — at zero
cost, zero latency, and zero vendor dependency.

## Independent benchmark 2 — agent tool-call risk (Jev does well)

Source: `github.com/themsquared/jev-benchmark`, n = 60, hand-labeled.

- **91.7% overall** — but decomposed: **100% on clear cases, 71.4% on ambiguous ones.**
- Calibration looked *good here*: the 0.9–1.0 confidence bin was 98% accurate, and every
  wrong answer arrived with hedged confidence (0.130–0.785). It never returned certainty
  while being wrong.
- Caveats from the authors themselves: n=60 is small, and an earlier run showed confidence
  saturating at exactly 1.000 on 5 of 6 easy cases.

Their design note is the best methodology advice in this whole dossier:

> "A benchmark of only obvious cases returns 100% and tells you nothing."

## Independent benchmark 3 — extraction (Every.to)

~25× faster and ~580× cheaper than Claude Fable 5.1 on a defect-detection passage task —
but Jev caught **6 of 7** planted defects where Fable caught **7 of 7**. The reviewer's own
verdict: good but not perfect, "a notch below the frontier", sample too small to draw a
production conclusion from.

## What all this adds up to

1. **Calibration quality is task-dependent, not a product property.** It was trustworthy on
   tool-call risk and worse-than-Haiku on phishing. You cannot know which case you are in
   without measuring *on your own data*. This is why an eval harness is not optional.
2. **Ambiguous cases are where it breaks.** 100% → 71.4% on the same task, same model, just
   harder examples. Your production traffic is mostly ambiguous cases.
3. **Answers are not deterministic.** 2.2% of identical repeated inputs got a different
   label. A "confidence" that moves between calls needs stability testing before you build
   an escalation path on it.
4. **Sometimes the right answer is a regex.** Ask whether calibration is genuinely your
   bottleneck before adding a vendor.

## The honest value proposition

Jev's edge is **latency, cost, and a typed interface that cannot break** — not accuracy.
That is a real and substantial edge: it makes judgment economically viable at volumes where
an LLM per item is absurd, and it deletes an entire class of parse-and-repair bugs. Adopt it
for those reasons. Do not adopt it believing it is more correct than a small LLM, because
the only independent head-to-head found says the opposite.

## Community suitability test

Use Jev only if you can answer yes to most of these (0–2 yeses → use different technology):

1. Is this a judgment, not a creation?
2. Is the answer space definable in advance?
3. Is it one atomic decision?
4. Does all the context it needs fit in state you can supply?
5. Could a human expert judge it in seconds?
6. Will software consume the result directly?
